acute illness = an illness that starts suddenly and is often severe but may be short
infectious disease = an illness caused by bacteria, viruses or other microbes that can spread
non-communicable disease = a long-term illness that is not passed from person to person, such as diabetes
contagious = able to spread from one person to another
outbreak = a sudden rise in cases of a disease in a place or group
epidemic = when a disease spreads quickly to many people in a region
pandemic = an epidemic that spreads across many countries or the whole world
immunity = the body’s ability to resist a particular infection
herd immunity = protection that appears when enough people in a group are immune
antibody = a protein the body makes to recognise and fight a specific germ
vaccination = giving a vaccine to protect someone from a disease
booster dose = an extra vaccine given later to strengthen protection
vaccine hesitancy = delay or refusal of a vaccine despite it being available
immunisation = the process of becoming protected against a disease, usually by vaccine
quarantine = keeping people who may be infected away from others for a set time
self-isolation = staying at home and away from others because you are ill or at risk
inflammation = the body’s painful, red or swollen reaction to injury or infection
autoimmune disease = an illness in which the immune system attacks the body’s own tissue
cardiovascular disease = illness of the heart and blood vessels
respiratory disease = illness of the lungs and airways
